meanings: nonstandard simplified variant of 鍾|钟[zhong1]

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锺 originally described a bronze cup or bell-shaped vessel, hence the metal radical.
重 (zhòng) gives the sound — 锺 is pronounced zhōng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā de xìng shì Zhōng.
example.english: His surname is Zhong.
example.fact: More than 85% of Han Chinese people share just 100 surnames, according to demographic studies — a legacy of the ancient 'Hundred Family Surnames' text long used to teach children to read.

components.note: 勹 (wrap/curl) — depicts a bent, crouching body posture, fitting 匍's meaning 'crawl, lie prone.'
甫 (fǔ) gives a sound close to 匍's reading pú — both belong to a family of characters (also including 浦, 圃) showing a historical p-/f- alternation.

example.pinyin: Yīng'ér huì púfú qiánjìn.
example.english: Babies can crawl forward.
example.fact: Crawling is a major developmental milestone, but some healthy babies skip it entirely and move straight from sitting to walking — a normal variation, according to pediatric researchers.

components.note: 礻 (spirit/altar) — ties 祗 to its meaning of religious respect and reverence.
氐 (dǐ) gives a sound only loosely related to 祗's reading zhī — the connection isn't obvious from modern pronunciation alone, and likely reflects an older sound shift.

example.pinyin: Tā zhī zūn fù mìng.
example.english: He respectfully obeyed his father's orders.
example.fact: The 礻 radical (a compressed form of 示, meaning 'altar/spirit') marks many characters related to worship and blessing, such as 福 (fortune), 祝 (to wish), and 祖 (ancestor).

components.note: 钅 (metal) — manganese is a metallic element.
孟 (mèng) gives the sound — 锰 is pronounced měng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Měng shì yī zhǒng jīnshǔ yuánsù.
example.english: Manganese is a metallic element.
example.fact: Manganese is essential for steel production — most manganese mined worldwide is used to strengthen steel and improve its resistance to wear.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 岌 describes a mountain peak that is high and steep.
及 (jí) gives the sound — 岌 is also pronounced jí, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò qiáo jíjí kěwēi.
example.english: This bridge is precariously close to collapse.
example.fact: 岌岌可危 is a four-character idiom (成语) literally meaning 'towering and dangerous' — Chinese has tens of thousands of such fixed idioms, many drawn from texts over 2,000 years old.

etymologyHint: Extra 余 food 饣; 余 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: The food radical (a compressed form of 食) ties the character to eating and provisions — fitting for a word about surplus food.
余 shares the exact same reading, yú, as this character — 馀 is in fact just a variant way of writing 余 in its 'surplus' sense.

example.pinyin: Nián nián yǒu yú.
example.english: May there be abundance every year.
example.fact: This New Year's greeting is often paired with fish imagery, because 鱼 (fish) is a near-homophone of 余/馀 (surplus) — which is why fish dishes are traditional at Chinese New Year dinners.

components.note: 田 (field) — 畹 is a traditional unit of land area.
宛 (wǎn) gives the sound — 畹 is also pronounced wǎn, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè piàn tiándì yuē yǒu yī wǎn.
example.english: This field is about one wan (a traditional land unit) in size.
example.fact: The mu (亩) is a traditional Chinese unit of land area still used today, roughly equal to 667 square meters, about one-fifteenth of a hectare — 畹 traditionally described a plot of 20 to 30 mu.

components.note: 米 (rice) — 糯 describes a sticky variety of rice.
需 (xū) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to nuò — compare 儒 (rú), which shares this same component and shows a similar divergence.

example.pinyin: Nuòmǐ zòngzi hěn hǎochī.
example.english: Glutinous rice zongzi are delicious.
example.fact: Zongzi, sticky rice dumplings wrapped in bamboo or reed leaves, are traditionally eaten at the Dragon Boat Festival to commemorate the poet Qu Yuan, who is said to have drowned himself in the Miluo River around 278 BC.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 胫 refers to the shinbone, a body part.

example.pinyin: Tā de jìnggǔ shòushāng le.
example.english: His shinbone was injured.
example.fact: The tibia (shinbone) is generally considered the second-longest weight-bearing bone in the human body, yet it is also one of the most commonly fractured bones in sports injuries.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 熠 describes something glowing or sparkling like flame.
習 (xí) gives a sound only loosely related to 熠's reading yì, sharing the final -i but not the initial consonant.

example.pinyin: Xīngxīng yìyì shēng huī.
example.english: The stars shine brilliantly.
example.fact: The starlight you see tonight may have left its source thousands or even millions of years ago, since light takes time to cross the vast distances of space.

etymologyHint: A bell 金 dangling from a tassel 亦

components.note: Metal — 銮 refers to small bronze bells that hung from an imperial carriage or horse harness.
Suggests the tassels or trappings the bells dangled from. It does not indicate the sound — 亦 is read yì, unrelated to luán.

example.pinyin: Huángdì zuò zhe luánjià chūxíng.
example.english: The emperor traveled about in his imperial carriage.
example.fact: In imperial China, small bronze bells called luan were attached to royal carriages and horse harnesses — their rhythmic jingling during travel was meant to enforce a steady, dignified pace and signal the emperor's approach.

meanings: name of a river in western Hunan that flows into Dongting lake
Yuan river in Guizhou and Hunan

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沅 names a river.
元 (yuán) gives the sound — 沅 is also pronounced yuán, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Yuán Jiāng liújīng Húnán.
example.english: The Yuan River flows through Hunan.
example.fact: The Yuan River is one of the four major rivers — along with the Xiang, Zi, and Li — that flow into Dongting Lake, China's second-largest freshwater lake.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 棣 names a flowering tree, the kerria.
隶 (lì) gives a sound close to 棣's reading dì — this phonetic series (also including 逮, dài) shows a historical l-/d- sound correspondence.

example.pinyin: Tángdì huā kāi de hěn měi.
example.english: The kerria flowers bloom beautifully.
example.fact: The flower 棠棣 (kerria) appears in the Book of Songs, China's oldest collection of poetry (roughly 11th–7th century BC), where it symbolizes brotherly affection.

meanings: banner or flag adorned with feathers

components.note: 方 (in characters like 旗, 旅, and 族, this component originally pictured a flag on a pole) — ties to 旌's meaning of a feathered banner.
生 (shēng) gives a sound only loosely related to 旌's reading jīng, sharing the nasal final -ng but differing in vowel and initial.

example.pinyin: Jūnduì jǔ zhe jīngqí qiánjìn.
example.english: The army advanced holding banners.
example.fact: In ancient Chinese warfare, colorful banners and flags were used to signal commands across the battlefield, since they could be seen over long distances amid the noise and chaos of combat.

components.note: 豆 (bean) — peas (豌豆) are a type of legume.
宛 (wǎn) gives the sound — 豌 is pronounced wān, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan chī wāndòu.
example.english: I like eating peas.
example.fact: The pea plant was central to Gregor Mendel's 19th-century breeding experiments on inheritance, which laid the foundation for the modern science of genetics.

components.note: 子 (child/seed) — a spore is a reproductive unit, conceptually like a seed or offspring.
包 (bāo) gives the sound — 孢 is also pronounced bāo, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Mógū tōngguò bāozǐ fánzhí.
example.english: Mushrooms reproduce through spores.
example.fact: A single mushroom can release trillions of spores over its lifetime, most too small to see individually, drifting on air currents to spread the fungus over long distances.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — radium is a metallic element.
雷 (léi) gives the sound — 镭 is also pronounced léi, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 镭是居里夫人发现的元素。
example.pinyin: Léi shì Jūlǐ fūrén fāxiàn de yuánsù.
example.english: Radium is an element discovered by Madame Curie.
example.fact: Marie Curie discovered radium in 1898 with her husband Pierre, and she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — physics and chemistry.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驸 originally related to an emperor's auxiliary carriage horses.
付 (fù) gives the sound — 驸 is also pronounced fù, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā chéng le huángdì de fùmǎ.
example.english: He became the emperor's son-in-law.
example.fact: In imperial China, the title 驸马 ('auxiliary horse') originally named an official in charge of the emperor's spare carriage horses, but from the Wei-Jin period onward it became the standard term for a princess's husband.

meanings: used in 腌臢|腌臜[a1 za1]
etymologyHint: Meat ⺼ left 奄 in salt; 奄 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: The flesh/meat radical (a form of 肉) — 腌 describes curing meat or vegetables in salt.
奄 is read yǎn, close to but not identical to yān — a reasonable, not exact, resemblance in sound.

example.pinyin: Māma yān le hěn duō xiáncài.
example.english: Mom pickled a lot of preserved vegetables.
example.fact: Pickling with salt is one of the oldest food preservation methods, used for thousands of years before refrigeration, because salt draws out water and inhibits the growth of most spoilage bacteria.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 盹 describes dozing, briefly closing one's eyes.
屯 (tún) gives a sound close to 盹's reading dǔn, sharing the final -un with closely related initial consonants.

example.pinyin: Tā zài kè shàng dǎdǔn.
example.english: He dozed off in class.
example.fact: Short naps of 10 to 20 minutes, sometimes called 'power naps,' can improve alertness and mental performance without causing the grogginess associated with longer naps.

components.note: 火 (fire) — ties to thermodynamics, the branch of physics concerned with heat, where entropy is a key concept.
商 (shāng) gives the sound — 熵 is also pronounced shāng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 熵是物理学中的重要概念。
example.pinyin: Shāng shì wùlǐxué zhōng de zhòngyào gàiniàn.
example.english: Entropy is an important concept in physics.
example.fact: The character 熵 was specially invented in 1923 to translate the English term 'entropy' — its fire radical 火 hints at thermodynamics, while its component 商 (shāng) gives the exact sound.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — a pick/mattock is a metal tool.
高 (gāo) gives the sound — 镐 is pronounced gǎo, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng gǎo wā dì.
example.english: He dug the ground with a pickaxe.
example.fact: 镐京 (Haojing), written with this same character, was the capital of the Western Zhou dynasty around 1046–771 BC, located near present-day Xi'an.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馐 refers to fine food, delicacies.
羞 (xiū) gives the sound — 馐 is also pronounced xiū, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 宴会上摆满了珍馐美味。
example.pinyin: Yànhuì shàng bǎi mǎn le zhēnxiū měiwèi.
example.english: The banquet table was covered with fine delicacies.
example.fact: Formal Chinese banquets have traditionally featured multiple courses served in a fixed order — sometimes eight, ten, or more dishes — to display hospitality and status.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — relates to the sound of calling or crying out.
婴 (yīng) gives the sound — 嘤 is also pronounced yīng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xiǎo niǎo yīngyīng de jiào.
example.english: The little bird chirped softly.
example.fact: The onomatopoeia 嘤嘤 appears in the ancient poem 伐木 from the Book of Songs, where birds calling to each other symbolizes people seeking friendship.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 癞 names a skin disease.
赖 (lài) gives the sound — 癞 is also pronounced lài, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Nà zhī làipí gǒu dàochù liúlàng.
example.english: That mangy dog wanders everywhere.
example.fact: Leprosy, historically feared and stigmatized, is actually one of the least contagious infectious diseases — over 95% of people exposed to the bacterium never develop the disease, according to the WHO.

etymologyHint: Tools 殳 made of bone 骨

components.note: Bone — dice were traditionally carved from bone or ivory before plastic became common.
Originally a pictograph of a hand-held tool or weapon; here it suggests the shaping/carving of the bone into a die. It is not a sound clue — 殳 is read shū, unrelated to tóu.

example.pinyin: Tā zhì tóuzi juédìng shùnxù.
example.english: He rolled the dice to decide the order.
example.fact: Dice are among the oldest gaming objects known, with six-sided dice found at archaeological sites in Iran and the Indus Valley dating back roughly 5,000 years.

etymologyHint: Chives 非 growing in the ground 一

components.note: 韭 is itself a pictograph: rows of leek leaves (the upper strokes) growing up out of a plot of ground, shown by the horizontal line at the base.

example.pinyin: Jiǔcài jiǎozi hěn xiāng.
example.english: Chive dumplings are very fragrant.
example.fact: Chives are a popular Chinese New Year dumpling filling partly because 韭 sounds like 久 (jiǔ, 'long-lasting'), making it an auspicious pun for a long life.

components.note: 门 (gate/door) — 阖 originally meant to close a door.
盍 (hé) gives the sound — 阖 is also pronounced hé, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhù dàjiā héjiā huānlè!
example.english: Wishing everyone a happy family reunion!
example.fact: 阖家欢乐 is a common New Year greeting meaning 'may your whole household be happy'; 阖 and its more common substitute 合 are near-homophones, so the phrase is often written 合家欢乐 instead.

etymologyHint: One's eyes 目at night 冥; 冥 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Eye — 瞑 specifically means to close one's eyes.
冥 shares the exact same reading, míng, as this character. It also contributes the sense of darkness/night, reinforcing the idea of closing one's eyes.

example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú kěyǐ míngmù le.
example.english: He can finally rest in peace.
example.fact: The phrase 死而瞑目 ('to close one's eyes in death without regret') describes someone who dies feeling their life's goals were fulfilled — a common expression of peaceful closure in Chinese literature.

etymologyHint: Clothing 衤 for the poor 卑; 卑 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: The clothing radical — 裨 originally referred to a supplementary layer sewn onto a garment, which is why its meaning extended to 'supplement, benefit.'
卑 is read bēi — only loosely similar to bì (same initial consonant, different vowel and tone), so this is an approximate resemblance at best, not a close match.

example.hanzi: 这次帮助对他大有裨益。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì bāngzhù duì tā dà yǒu bìyì.
example.english: This help was of great benefit to him.
example.fact: 裨 originally referred to a supplementary layer sewn onto a garment for extra warmth, which is why it carries the clothing radical 衤; the meaning later extended metaphorically to 'benefit, supplement.'

etymologyHint: A tunnel 宀 made in stone 石

components.note: The roof/dwelling radical here represents an overhead covering, i.e. the roof of a cave or tunnel.
Stone — the tunnel or quarry is dug into rock. 石 is read shí and is not phonetically related to dàng.

example.pinyin: Huìyì bèi yándàng le yī zhōu.
example.english: The meeting was postponed by a week.
example.fact: 宕 originally meant a cave or stone quarry cut into a mountainside (the roof radical 宀 over 石, 'stone'); its modern sense of 'delay, put off' developed later as a separate extended meaning.

etymologyHint: A dog 犬 that won't come indoors 户

components.note: Door/household — represents a home or dwelling.
A dog that refuses to come indoors — a picture of stubborn, unruly behavior that gave rise to the meaning 'perverse, rebellious.'

example.pinyin: Tā píqi bàolì.
example.english: His temperament is fierce and violent.
example.fact: 暴戾恣睢 is a four-character idiom describing extreme cruelty and lawlessness, drawn from classical Chinese texts describing tyrannical rulers.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — engraving is often done into metal (or stone) with a metal tool.
隽 (juàn) gives the sound — 镌 is pronounced juān, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 工匠在石碑上镌刻文字。
example.pinyin: Gōngjiàng zài shíbēi shàng juānkè wénzì.
example.english: The craftsman engraved characters onto the stone tablet.
example.fact: Stone stelae engraved with calligraphy have been used in China for over two thousand years to record histories, honor the dead, and preserve famous handwriting styles for later generations to study.

etymologyHint: A gloomy 冥 rainy 氵 day

components.note: Water — refers to rain or the sea.
冥 shares the exact same reading, míng, as this character. It also contributes the meaning of darkness/gloom.

example.pinyin: Zhuāngzǐ lǐ de Běimíng yǒu yī tiáo dà yú.
example.english: In the Zhuangzi, there is a giant fish in the Northern Sea.
example.fact: The opening chapter of the Daoist classic Zhuangzi (4th century BC) begins with a giant fish in the Northern Sea that transforms into an enormous bird called Peng, one of the most famous images in Chinese philosophical literature.

components.note: 片 (slice/plank) — ancient documents were written on wooden slips or tablets.

卖 (mài) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to dú — compare 读/犊 (both dú), which share this same component and reading, suggesting a historical connection now obscured by sound change.

example.pinyin: Gǔdài guānyuán àndú láoxíng.
example.english: Ancient officials were worn out by their paperwork.
example.fact: Before paper became widespread, documents were often written on wooden tablets called 牍; the phrase 案牍劳形 ('worn out by official documents') comes from the Tang poet Liu Yuxi's famous essay 陋室铭.

etymologyHint: Someone aiming a bow 乃 at a small bird 隹

components.note: A short-tailed bird — 隽 originally meant a plump, choice game bird, a sense later extended metaphorically to 'outstanding, superior.'
A curved shape, traditionally explained as a snare or hooked tool used to catch the bird. It is not a sound clue — 乃 is read nǎi, unrelated to juàn.

example.pinyin: Zhè piān sǎnwén yìwèi juànyǒng.
example.english: This essay has a lasting, profound meaning.
example.fact: 隽 has two readings in Mandarin — juàn, as in 隽永 ('meaningful and lasting'), and jùn, used in some proper names — a common feature in Chinese called 多音字, characters with multiple pronunciations.

components.note: 女 (woman) — reflects the gender-specific reference of the term.
表 (biǎo) gives the sound — 婊 is also pronounced biǎo, an exact match.

example.hanzi: "婊"是一个带侵犯性的贬义词。
example.pinyin: "Biǎo" shì yī gè dài qīnfànxìng de biǎnyìcí.
example.english: "Biao" is an offensive, derogatory term.
example.fact: In modern Mandarin internet slang, attaching 婊 to a descriptive term (as in 绿茶婊, 'green tea biǎo') creates a mocking label for a type of person seen as fake — a word-formation pattern that spread widely online in the early 2010s.

meanings: center or bull's eye of an archery target (old)

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹄 can mean 'swan.'
告 (gào) gives a sound close to 鹄's reading gǔ, sharing the initial g- though the final vowel has shifted.

example.pinyin: Tā cóngxiǎo jiù yǒu hónghú zhī zhì.
example.english: Since childhood he has had grand ambitions.
example.fact: 鸿鹄之志 ('the ambition of a swan goose') comes from a story in the Records of the Grand Historian about the rebel leader Chen Sheng, who told his fellow laborers that great people's ambitions cannot be understood by ordinary sparrows.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 埂 describes a raised ridge of earth.
更 (gēng) gives the sound — 埂 is pronounced gěng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín yán zhe tiángěng zǒu.
example.english: The farmer walked along the field ridge.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese rice farming, raised earthen ridges called 田埂 divide flooded paddies into separate plots, letting farmers control water levels precisely for each section.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拄 describes propping oneself up by hand, as with a cane.
主 (zhǔ) gives the sound — 拄 is also pronounced zhǔ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Lǎorén zhǔ zhe guǎizhàng zǒulù.
example.english: The old man walked leaning on a cane.
example.fact: Physical therapists generally recommend holding a cane on the side opposite an injured or weak leg, rather than the same side, because it better mimics natural walking mechanics.

meanings: the mythological sister and successor to Fuxi
sister of legendary emperor Fuxi 伏羲[Fu2 xi1]

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娲 names the mythological goddess Nüwa.
呙 (here read wāi) gives a sound close to 娲's reading wā.

example.pinyin: Nǚwā yòng nítǔ zào rén.
example.english: Nüwa created humans out of clay.
example.fact: In Chinese mythology, the goddess Nüwa is credited with molding humanity out of yellow clay and, after a great catastrophe, repairing a damaged sky using five-colored stones.

components.note: Relates 虬 to the category of legendary serpent-like creatures — here, a young, hornless dragon.
A curling stroke that pictures the coiled, curved body of the young dragon.

example.pinyin: Tā liú zhe qiúxū.
example.english: He has a curly beard.
example.fact: In classical Chinese art, dragons were often depicted with coiling, serpentine bodies, and the character 虬 specifically describes anything curled like a young, hornless dragon.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 萱 names the day-lily.
宣 (xuān) gives the sound — 萱 is also pronounced xuān, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xuāncǎo shì mǔqīn de xiàngzhēng.
example.english: The day-lily is a symbol of one's mother.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese culture, the day-lily is a symbolic flower for one's mother, much as the carnation is for Western Mother's Day — the term 萱堂 ('day-lily hall') is a poetic way to refer to one's mother.

etymologyHint: The sound 口 of ripples in the water 波; 波 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Mouth — marks the character as a sound/spoken particle rather than a concrete noun.
波 is read bō, very close to the neutral-toned bo, hinting strongly at the pronunciation.

example.pinyin: Shuǐpào bōbō de xiǎng.
example.english: The bubbles went "bo bo" as they popped.
example.fact: Mandarin has a rich set of onomatopoeic characters built from the mouth radical 口 to signal that a character represents a sound rather than a concrete meaning, including 啪 (clap), 嘭 (bang), and 啵 (a soft pop).

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蠡 names a wood-boring insect.
彖 (tuàn) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to lí.

example.hanzi: 这只是管窥蠡测，未必全面。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǐshì guānkuī lící, wèibì quánmiàn.
example.english: This is just a narrow glimpse, not necessarily the full picture.
example.fact: The idiom 管窥蠡测 combines two images for limited perspective: 管窥 ('viewing through a narrow tube') and 蠡测 ('measuring the sea with a gourd ladle') — both suggest that a small tool gives only a fragmentary understanding of something vast.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — taro (芋) is a plant.
于 (yú) gives the sound — 芋 is pronounced yù, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Yùtou zuò de tiánpǐn hěn hǎochī.
example.english: Desserts made from taro are delicious.
example.fact: Taro is one of the oldest cultivated crops in the world, grown for its starchy root across tropical and subtropical Asia and the Pacific Islands for thousands of years.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — rouge (胭脂) was applied to the skin of the face.
因 (yīn) gives a sound close to 胭's reading yān.

example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng tú le yānzhi.
example.english: She applied rouge on her face.
example.fact: Rouge has been used as a cosmetic in China for over two thousand years; early versions were made from crushed safflower petals mixed with fat to create a red pigment for the cheeks and lips.

components.note: 豸 (a radical used broadly for beasts) — 豺 names the jackal.
才 (cái) gives a sound close to 豺's reading chái, sharing the final -ai.

example.pinyin: Cháiláng shì xiōngměng de yěshòu.
example.english: Jackals and wolves are fierce wild beasts.
example.fact: The idiom 豺狼当道 ('jackals and wolves block the road') is a classical metaphor for cruel officials or tyrants dominating a government, used in Chinese political writing for centuries.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — relates to speech, since 啻 ('merely, only') is a spoken qualifier.
帝 (dì) gives a sound only loosely related to 啻's reading chì, sharing the final -i.

example.hanzi: 这份礼物不啻是雪中送炭。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn lǐwù bùchì shì xuězhōngsòngtàn.
example.english: This gift is nothing less than help arriving exactly when needed.
example.fact: The idiom 雪中送炭 ('sending charcoal in the snow') describes providing crucial help exactly when someone needs it most, since charcoal for heating would be most valuable during a snowstorm.

meanings: used in 襤褸|褴褛[lan2 lu : 3]

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 褛 describes tattered clothing.
娄 (lóu) gives a sound close to 褛's reading lǚ — compare 屡 (lǚ), which shares this same component and a similar reading shift.

example.pinyin: Tā yīshān lánlǚ.
example.english: His clothes were ragged and tattered.
example.fact: 衣衫褴褛 is a common description in Chinese literature for extreme poverty, and both 褴 and 褛 share the clothing radical 衤, since they exist almost exclusively together as this one fixed compound.

components.note: 虫 (insect/worm) — 蛆 names the maggot.
且 (qiě) gives a sound close to 蛆's reading qū, sharing the initial q-.

example.pinyin: Lājī duī lǐ yǒu hěn duō qū.
example.english: There are many maggots in the trash heap.
example.fact: Maggots, the larvae of flies, are used in a modern medical treatment called maggot debridement therapy, where sterile maggots clean dead tissue from wounds that resist healing.

meanings: used in 檸檬|柠檬[ning2 meng2]

components.note: 木 (tree) — lemon (柠檬) grows on a tree.
宁 (níng) gives the sound — 柠 is also pronounced níng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Níngméng wèidào hěn suān.
example.english: Lemon tastes very sour.
example.fact: Lemons contain roughly 5% citric acid, which gives them their characteristically sour taste and also makes them useful as a natural cleaning agent.

meanings: to break off or break open sth with one's hands
etymologyHint: To tear something 分 with both hands 手

components.note: Two hands, one on each side of the character, grip and pull in opposite directions.
Means 'to divide, separate' — placed between the two hands, it depicts the actual act of tearing something apart.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ miànbāo bāi chéng liǎng bàn.
example.english: He broke the bread into two halves.
example.fact: 掰 is a rare example of a Chinese character built like a diagram: two hands (手) flank 分 ('divide') in the middle, visually depicting the action of tearing something apart by hand.

meanings: the small seal 小篆 and great seal 大篆

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient seal-script texts were carved onto bamboo strips.
彖 (tuàn) gives a sound close to 篆's reading zhuàn, sharing the final -uan.

example.hanzi: 篆书是最古老的汉字字体之一。
example.pinyin: Zhuànshū shì zuì gǔlǎo de Hànzì zìtǐ zhī yī.
example.english: Seal script is one of the oldest styles of Chinese characters.
example.fact: Seal script was the standard writing style of the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) and is still used today for carving traditional name seals, which function like a signature on Chinese documents and artworks.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 倌 names a person with a specific, usually humble, job.
官 (guān) gives the sound — 倌 is also pronounced guān, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Cūn lǐ yǒu ge fàngniúguān.
example.english: There's a cowherd in the village.
example.fact: The suffix 倌 attaches to job names for someone tending animals or performing a humble trade, as in 牛倌 (cowherd) — it carries the person radical 亻 since it denotes a role filled by a person.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咛 relates to speaking, verbal instruction.
宁 (níng) gives the sound — 咛 is also pronounced níng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 妈妈再三叮咛我要小心。
example.pinyin: Māma zàisān dīngníng wǒ yào xiǎoxīn.
example.english: Mom repeatedly reminded me to be careful.
example.fact: 叮咛 is used specifically for repeated, caring verbal reminders, often from a parent to a child before a trip or exam — both of its characters share the mouth radical 口.

components.note: 虫 (worm) — 蛭 names the leech.
至 (zhì) gives the sound — 蛭 is also pronounced zhì, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shuǐzhì shēnghuó zài chítáng lǐ.
example.english: Leeches live in ponds.
example.fact: Leeches secrete a natural anticoagulant called hirudin in their saliva, which keeps their host's blood from clotting while they feed — a compound now studied for use in modern anti-clotting medicines.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the connection to 谡's core meaning ('to rise, to be composed') is not obvious; radicals sometimes reflect an older sense now obscured by semantic drift.
畟 (cè) gives a sound only loosely related to 谡's reading sù, sharing a sibilant-adjacent initial.

example.pinyin: Mǎ Sù shīshǒu le Jiētíng.
example.english: Ma Su lost control of Jieting.
example.fact: Ma Su was a Three Kingdoms-period general whose failure to defend Jieting led the strategist Zhuge Liang to execute him despite their friendship — a historical episode recorded in Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms.

meanings: used in 蕁麻|荨麻[qian2 ma2]

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 荨 names the nettle.
寻 (xún) gives the sound — 荨 is also pronounced xún, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xúnmá de yèzi yǒu dú cì.
example.english: Nettle leaves have stinging spines.
example.fact: Stinging nettle leaves are covered with tiny hollow hairs that act like hypodermic needles, injecting chemicals such as histamine and formic acid when touched, causing the plant's characteristic stinging rash.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 莞 names an aquatic herb, the clubrush.
完 (wán) gives a sound only loosely related to 莞's reading guǎn, sharing the final -an.

example.hanzi: 东莞是广东的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Dōngguǎn shì Guǎngdōng de yī gè chéngshì.
example.english: Dongguan is a city in Guangdong.
example.fact: Dongguan, a city whose name uses this character, grew from a market town into one of the world's major manufacturing hubs, sometimes nicknamed the 'World's Factory' for its concentration of electronics and toy production.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 澹 can describe calm, still water.
詹 (zhān) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to dàn.

example.hanzi: 诸葛亮说："非淡泊无以明志。"
example.pinyin: Zhūgě Liàng shuō: "Fēi dànbó wú yǐ míng zhì."
example.english: Zhuge Liang said, "Without indifference to worldly gain, one cannot clarify one's ambitions."
example.fact: This famous line comes from Zhuge Liang's letter to his son, 《诫子书》; 澹 is often used interchangeably with the more common 淡 in this same word, 澹泊/淡泊, meaning indifference to fame and wealth.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 纭 describes a tangle of numerous, confused threads, a metaphor for disorder.
云 (yún) gives the sound — 纭 is also pronounced yún, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Guānyú zhè jiàn shì, zhòng shuō fēnyún.
example.english: Regarding this matter, opinions vary widely.
example.fact: 众说纷纭 ('many people, many differing opinions') is a common idiom in Chinese news writing whenever there is no clear consensus on a controversial topic.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 潞 names a river.
路 (lù) gives the sound — 潞 is also pronounced lù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 潞河曾是重要的水运通道。
example.pinyin: Lù Hé céng shì zhòngyào de shuǐyùn tōngdào.
example.english: The Lu River was once an important water transport route.
example.fact: 潞州, an ancient administrative region named after this river and located in what is now Shanxi province, was an important prefecture during the Tang dynasty.

meanings: to go up to. flourishing a superlative

components.note: 阝 (place, from 邑 'city/region') — 郅 relates to a place name and, separately, to an intensifier meaning 'extremely.'
至 (zhì) gives the sound — 郅 is also pronounced zhì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 郅支单于最终被汉朝军队击败。
example.pinyin: Zhìzhī Chányú zuìzhōng bèi Hàncháo jūnduì jíbài.
example.english: Chanyu Zhizhi was ultimately defeated by the Han dynasty's army.
example.fact: Zhizhi, a Xiongnu chieftain defeated by Han forces in 36 BC, is remembered for provoking the line 'even from afar, those who offend the mighty Han will surely be punished,' still quoted today to express resolve against distant threats.

etymologyHint: Picture of an arrow shot from a bow

example.pinyin: Gǔrén yìshè fēiqín.
example.english: Ancient people hunted birds by shooting corded arrows.
example.fact: 弋 originally referred to a hunting technique using an arrow tied to a cord, letting the hunter retrieve both the arrow and the fallen bird — a method described in classical texts like the Book of Songs.

components.note: 风 (wind) — 飕 describes the sound of wind blowing.
叟 (sǒu) gives the sound — 飕 is pronounced sōu, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Lěngfēng sōusōu de chuīguò.
example.english: A cold wind whooshed past.
example.fact: The sensation of a cold wind feeling colder than the actual air temperature is called wind chill — moving air strips away the thin layer of warm air next to your skin faster than still air does.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 螳 names the praying mantis.
堂 (táng) gives the sound — 螳 is also pronounced táng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tángláng shì nóngtián lǐ de yìchóng.
example.english: Mantises are beneficial insects in farmland.
example.fact: The idiom 螳臂当车 ('a mantis blocking a chariot with its arm') describes a hopeless attempt to stop something far more powerful than oneself, drawn from the ancient philosophical text Zhuangzi.

etymologyHint: A man ⺼ wearing a helmet 由

components.note: Traditionally explained as resembling the rounded shape of an ancient helmet or cap.
Represents the person wearing the helmet beneath it. 由 is read yóu and is not phonetically related to zhòu.

example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen shēn chuān jiǎzhòu.
example.english: The soldiers wore armor and helmets.
example.fact: 甲胄 ('armor and helmet') is a classical compound for a complete suit of battle gear; 胄 alone can also mean 'descendants,' as in 贵胄 ('noble descendants'), an unrelated extended sense.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蟑 names the cockroach.
章 (zhāng) gives the sound — 蟑 is also pronounced zhāng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ yǒu yī zhī zhāngláng.
example.english: There's a cockroach in the kitchen.
example.fact: Cockroaches are remarkably resilient insects — some species can survive for weeks without food and can hold their breath underwater for around 30 to 40 minutes.

components.note: 犭 (dog/animal) — several characters describing base or unrefined behavior use the dog radical.
畏 (wèi) gives the sound — 猥 is pronounced wěi, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā de yányǔ hěn wěisuǒ.
example.english: His words were vulgar and unseemly.
example.fact: 猥 combines the dog radical 犭 with a phonetic component; several characters describing base or unrefined behavior in Chinese use the dog radical, reflecting old cultural associations between certain animals and moral judgment.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宓 conveys a sense of quiet, sheltered stillness.
必 (bì) gives a sound close to 宓's reading mì, sharing the final -i and a related bilabial initial.

example.pinyin: Tā xìng Mì.
example.english: His surname is Mi.
example.fact: 宓 is a rare surname today, but it is historically linked to the mythological sage-king Fuxi, who in some ancient texts was also referred to as 宓羲, using this alternate character for his name.

etymologyHint: The sun 日 hidden behind a cloud 云

components.note: Sun.
Cloud — the sun hidden behind clouds gives the meaning 'overcast, cloudy.' 云 is read yún, not phonetically close to tán.

example.pinyin: Tā de chénggōng rú tánhuā yī xiàn.
example.english: His success was as fleeting as a night-blooming flower.
example.fact: 昙花一现 describes something spectacular but short-lived; the epiphyllum cactus flower it refers to actually blooms for just a few hours at night before wilting, a vivid natural metaphor for fleeting glory.

meanings: ancient weapon like a long solid metal truncheon

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锏 names a metal weapon.
间 (jiān) gives the sound — 锏 is pronounced jiǎn, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 古代武将常用锏作为兵器。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài wǔjiàng chángyòng jiǎn zuòwéi bīngqì.
example.english: Ancient generals often used the jian as a weapon.
example.fact: The 锏 is a traditional Chinese blunt weapon shaped like a straight, four-sided metal rod without a cutting edge, historically used to crush armor rather than slice through it.

components.note: 虫 (creature radical, used broadly) — 蟠 describes a coiled dragon or snake.
番 (fān) gives a sound close to 蟠's reading pán — this phonetic series shows the historical p-/f- alternation (compare 潘, pān).

example.pinyin: Cípíng shàng huà zhe pánlóng.
example.english: A coiled dragon is painted on the porcelain vase.
example.fact: The coiled dragon is a recurring motif in Chinese imperial art, often circling a pillar, vase, or ceiling — symbolizing power held in reserve, since a coiled dragon can strike at any moment.

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 過/过's core meaning is 'to pass through.'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 過's reading guò, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā měitiān jīngguò zhèlǐ.
example.english: He passes by here every day.
example.fact: 過 is the traditional form of 过 ('to pass'); mainland China adopted simplified characters through reforms in the 1950s and 1960s, while Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau continue to use traditional forms like 過 today.

etymologyHint: A tree 木 bearing sweet fruit 甘; 甘 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Tree — refers to the tangerine tree.
甘 shares the exact same reading, gān, as this character. It also means 'sweet,' describing the fruit's taste.

example.pinyin: Gānjú fùhán wéishēngsù C.
example.english: Citrus fruits are rich in vitamin C.
example.fact: British sailors in the 18th century began carrying citrus fruit on long voyages after physician James Lind's experiments showed it could prevent scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency.

components.note: 火 (fire) — chemistry characters for hydrocarbon gases conventionally use the fire radical.
希 (xī) gives the sound — 烯 is also pronounced xī, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 乙烯是重要的化工原料。
example.pinyin: Yǐxī shì zhòngyào de huàgōng yuánliào.
example.english: Ethylene is an important chemical raw material.
example.fact: Ethylene is the most widely produced organic compound in the world by volume, serving as the building block for polyethylene, the most common type of plastic.

components.note: 勹 (wrap/curl) — depicts a crouching, prone body posture.
畐 (fú) gives the sound — 匐 is also pronounced fú, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 士兵匍匐前进躲避炮火。
example.pinyin: Shìbīng púfú qiánjìn duǒbì pàohuǒ.
example.english: The soldier crawled forward to avoid gunfire.
example.fact: Crawling with the body kept low is a basic technique taught in militaries worldwide to minimize a soldier's exposure to enemy fire.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 濮 names a river.
僕 (pú) gives the sound — 濮 is also pronounced pú, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 濮阳有"中华第一龙"的美誉。
example.pinyin: Púyáng yǒu "Zhōnghuá dì yī lóng" de měiyù.
example.english: Puyang is known by the nickname "China's First Dragon."
example.fact: In 1987, archaeologists at Puyang excavated a dragon-and-tiger mosaic made of clam shells dated to roughly 6,400 years ago, among the earliest known dragon images in Chinese culture.

meanings: used in 蛐蟮[qu1 shan5] and 曲蟮[qu1 shan5]

components.note: 虫 (worm) — 蟮 names a type of earthworm.
善 (shàn) gives the sound — 蟮 is also pronounced shàn, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 蟮虫在泥土里钻来钻去。
example.pinyin: Shànchóng zài nítǔ lǐ zuān lái zuān qù.
example.english: Earthworms burrow back and forth in the soil.
example.fact: Earthworms aerate soil and break down organic matter — Charles Darwin spent decades studying them and, in 1881, published his final book entirely devoted to their effect on soil formation.

components.note: The spirit/altar radical (a compressed form of 示) marks this as a word about divine or religious matters — here, divine protection.
右 shares the exact same reading, yòu, as this character.

example.hanzi: 他名叫天祐，意思是上天保佑。
example.pinyin: Tā míng jiào Tiānyòu, yìsi shì shàngtiān bǎoyòu.
example.english: His name is Tianyou, meaning "blessed by heaven."
example.fact: 祐 and its more common counterpart 佑 (both meaning 'divine blessing') are frequently used in Chinese given names, reflecting a long tradition of choosing names that invoke protection or good fortune.

etymologyHint: A man 人 taking shelter in a lean-to 厂

components.note: A cliff or lean-to shelter.
A person bent over beneath the slanting shelter — a picture that gave rise to the meaning 'tilted, oblique.'

example.pinyin: Xiě shī yào zhùyì píngzè.
example.english: When writing poetry, one must pay attention to level and oblique tones.
example.fact: Classical Chinese poetry follows strict patterns of 平 (level tones) and 仄 (oblique tones) that alternate in fixed positions within a line — a tonal rule central to genres like Tang-dynasty regulated verse.

example.pinyin: Chánshī niàn le yī shǒu jìyǔ.
example.english: The Zen master recited a Buddhist verse.
example.fact: 偈 comes from the Sanskrit word 'gāthā' and refers to short verses used in Buddhist scripture to summarize teachings in a memorable, often rhythmic form.

meanings: marine monster which can change its shape

components.note: 虫 (a radical used broadly for creatures, including mollusks) — 蜃 names a mythical shape-shifting sea creature.
辰 (chén) gives a sound close to 蜃's reading shèn, sharing the final -en and a similar retroflex initial.

example.hanzi: 沙漠中出现了海市蜃楼。
example.pinyin: Shāmò zhōng chūxiàn le hǎishìshènlóu.
example.english: A mirage appeared in the desert.
example.fact: 海市蜃楼 ('sea market, mirage tower') describes a mirage; ancient Chinese folklore attributed the illusion to a giant shape-shifting sea creature called 蜃 breathing out vapors that formed phantom cities.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 箴 originally referred to a bamboo or bone needle.
咸 (xián) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to zhēn.

example.hanzi: 这是一句很有智慧的箴言。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yī jù hěn yǒu zhìhuì de zhēnyán.
example.english: This is a very wise maxim.
example.fact: 箴言 is also the Chinese title of the Book of Proverbs in the Bible, chosen because 箴 originally meant a needle used for sewing and, metaphorically, for 'pricking' people toward good behavior.

components.note: 巛 (river/stream, a pictograph of flowing water) — 粼 describes the sparkle of clear water.
粦 (lín) gives the sound — 粼 is also pronounced lín, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Hú miàn bōguāng línlín.
example.english: The lake's surface shimmers with rippling light.
example.fact: 波光粼粼 is a common four-character description in Chinese nature writing for sunlight sparkling on rippling water, often used in poetry to evoke a tranquil scene.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗥 describes howling or crying out loud.
皋 (gāo) gives a sound close to 嗥's reading háo, sharing the final -ao.

example.pinyin: Yè lǐ chuánlái láng háo shēng.
example.english: At night, the sound of wolves howling could be heard.
example.fact: Wolves howl to communicate over long distances — a howl can be heard by other wolves several kilometers away in open terrain, helping packs coordinate location and territory.

meanings: used in 襤褸|褴褛[lan2 lu : 3]

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 褴 describes ragged, tattered clothing.
监 (jiān) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to lán.

example.hanzi: 尽管衣衫褴褛，他依然保持着尊严。
example.pinyin: Jǐnguǎn yīshān lánlǚ, tā yīrán bǎochí zhe zūnyán.
example.english: Despite being dressed in rags, he still maintained his dignity.
example.fact: 褴 and 褛 form one of many Chinese 联绵词 (binomial compounds) that must always appear together and cannot be understood separately — similar to how 'ram' and 'shackle' carry no meaning alone in English 'ramshackle.'

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 蕨 names the fern/bracken.
厥 (jué) gives the sound — 蕨 is also pronounced jué, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Juélèi zhíwù méiyǒu huā.
example.english: Ferns don't have flowers.
example.fact: Ferns are among the oldest plant groups on Earth, appearing in the fossil record more than 350 million years ago, long before flowering plants evolved.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 蓟 names the thistle.

makemeahanzi lists 鱼 (yú) as part of the phonetic element, though on its own 鱼 isn't obviously close to 蓟's reading jì — the phonetic contribution likely comes from the fuller combination 鱼+刂, not 鱼 alone.

example.hanzi: 蓟是古代北京地区的名称。
example.pinyin: Jì shì gǔdài Běijīng dìqū de míngchēng.
example.english: Ji was the ancient name for the Beijing region.
example.fact: 蓟 was the name of an ancient state and city located in what is now Beijing during the Zhou dynasty, roughly the 11th century to 222 BC — one of the earliest recorded names associated with the site of China's modern capital.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 圩 describes an earthen embankment or dike.
于 (yú) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to wéi.

example.pinyin: Cūnmín xiūjiàn wéidī fánghóng.
example.english: Villagers built dikes to prevent flooding.
example.fact: 圩田 ('polder fields') are a traditional Chinese technique in the Yangtze and Pearl River deltas where low-lying land is enclosed by earthen dikes and drained for farming, similar in concept to Dutch polders.

etymologyHint: Giving birth to a second 亦 child 子

components.note: Child.
Originally suggested something paired or doubled, contributing to the meaning 'twins.' 亦 is read yì, not phonetically related to luán.

example.pinyin: Tā shēng le yī duì luánshēng jiěmèi.
example.english: She gave birth to a pair of twin sisters.
example.fact: Identical twins, called 同卵孪生 in Chinese ('same-egg twins'), develop from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos, which is why they share nearly identical DNA.

etymologyHint: The sun 日 setting below the woods 木

components.note: Trees/woods.
Sun — pictured sinking below the treetops, an image of something disappearing from sight, hence 'obscure, vanished.'

example.pinyin: Tā líkāi hòu jiù yǎo wú yīnxìn.
example.english: After he left, there was no news of him at all.
example.fact: 杳 pictures the sun (日) disappearing below the treetops (木) — a visual image of something sinking out of sight, which is why the character came to mean 'vanished' or 'obscure.'

components.note: 鬼 (ghost) — a nightmare (魇) was traditionally blamed on a ghost or spirit.
厌 (yàn) gives the sound — 魇 is pronounced yǎn, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā zuówǎn zuò le yī gè mèngyǎn.
example.english: He had a nightmare last night.
example.fact: The English word 'nightmare' originally referred to a demon believed to sit on a sleeper's chest, not a horse — a folk belief echoed in the Chinese term 梦魇, whose 魇 also names a ghost blamed for bad dreams.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 荤 originally referred to pungent vegetables like garlic and onion.
军 (jūn) gives a sound close to 荤's reading hūn, sharing the final -un.

example.pinyin: Tā chīsù, bù chī hūncài.
example.english: He's a vegetarian and doesn't eat meat dishes.
example.fact: 荤 originally referred to pungent vegetables like garlic and onions rather than meat; its meaning shifted to 'meat dishes' over time as Buddhist dietary rules against strong-smelling vegetables shaped everyday usage.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诿 involves verbally shifting blame onto someone else.
委 (wěi) gives the sound — 诿 is also pronounced wěi, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā zǒng shì tuīwěi zérèn.
example.english: He always shirks responsibility.
example.fact: 推诿 combines 推 ('to push') and 诿 ('to shift blame'), vividly depicting the act of pushing responsibility onto someone else — a common compounding pattern where near-synonyms combine to strengthen meaning.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — early hairpins were often carved from bamboo.
朁 (cǎn) gives a sound close to 簪's reading zān, sharing the final -an and a related affricate initial.

example.pinyin: Gǔdài nǚzǐ yòng zānzi pán fà.
example.english: Ancient women used hairpins to style their hair.
example.fact: In ancient China, a girl's coming-of-age ceremony at fifteen was marked by pinning up her hair for the first time — a ritual called 笄礼, using a closely related hairpin character (笄) — paralleling the male capping ceremony at twenty.

meanings: used in 氤氳|氤氲[yin1 yun1]

components.note: 气 (vapor/air) — 氲 describes swirling mist or vapor.
昷 (wēn) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to yūn — compare 温 (wēn), which shares this same original component.

example.pinyin: Shāngǔ zhōng yúnwù yīnyūn.
example.english: Mist and clouds swirl hazily in the valley.
example.fact: 氤氲, describing swirling mist or a rich atmosphere, appears in the ancient Book of Changes to describe the blending of yin and yang forces said to give rise to all things in the universe.

etymologyHint: To pile up 累 by hand 扌; 累 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand — the stacking action is done by hand.
Means 'to pile up, accumulate,' directly matching 摞's meaning. Its reading lěi is not a close match to luò, so it contributes meaning here, not sound.

example.pinyin: Zhuō shàng fàng zhe yī luò shū.
example.english: There's a stack of books on the table.
example.fact: 摞 functions as both a verb ('to stack') and a measure word for stacked objects, as in 一摞书 ('a stack of books') — Chinese has dozens of specialized measure words that describe the shape of what's being counted.

components.note: 风 (wind) — 飒 imitates the sound of wind.
立 (lì) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to sà.

example.hanzi: 她英姿飒爽地走进会场。
example.pinyin: Tā yīngzī sàshuǎng de zǒujìn huìchǎng.
example.english: She strode into the meeting hall with a dashing, spirited bearing.
example.fact: 飒 is built around the component 风 ('wind'), since the character originally imitated the swishing sound of wind — a sound image later extended to describe someone moving with brisk, energetic vigor.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 镂 describes carving or engraving into metal.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — 镂 is pronounced lòu, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 这个木盒上有镂空花纹。
example.pinyin: Zhège mù hé shàng yǒu lòukōng huāwén.
example.english: This wooden box has openwork carved patterns.
example.fact: 镂空 ('hollow carving') is a traditional Chinese decorative technique where material is carved all the way through to create an openwork pattern, used in paper-cutting as well as jade and wood carving.

meanings: to ladle out; to scoop up
etymologyHint: A hand 爫 fetching food from a container 臼

components.note: A hand (claw shape) reaching down.
A mortar or container — the hand is scooping something out of it, giving the meaning 'to ladle, scoop.'

example.pinyin: Tā yòng sháozi yǎo tāng.
example.english: He scooped soup with a spoon.
example.fact: 舀 pictures a hand (爫) reaching into a mortar or container (臼) to scoop something out — a simple but vivid combination for the action of ladling.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ duōnián de sùyuàn.
example.english: This is my long-cherished wish of many years.
example.fact: 夙愿 ('long-held wish') and 夙敌 ('longtime rival') both use 夙 in its extended sense of 'from long ago,' even though the character's core original meaning referred specifically to early morning.

components.note: 臣 (minister/official) — 臧 can describe upright conduct, as expected of a good official, and is also a surname.
戕 (qiāng) gives a sound only loosely related to 臧's reading zāng, sharing the final -ang.

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zāngpǐ rénwù.
example.english: He likes to judge and critique people's character.
example.fact: 臧否人物 ('to appraise people's character') was a popular pastime among scholars in the Wei-Jin period (3rd–4th century AD), when public character assessments could significantly influence a person's official career.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 蒿 names mugwort/wormwood.
高 (gāo) gives a sound close to 蒿's reading hāo, sharing the final -ao.

example.hanzi: 青蒿素是从黄花蒿中提取的。
example.pinyin: Qīnghāosù shì cóng huánghuāhāo zhōng tíqǔ de.
example.english: Artemisinin is extracted from sweet wormwood.
example.fact: Artemisinin, an anti-malarial drug derived from the wormwood plant, was discovered by Chinese scientist Tu Youyou, who won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for a discovery that has saved millions of lives.

components.note: 豸 (a radical used broadly for beasts) — 貂 names the marten/sable.
召 (zhào) gives a sound only loosely related to 貂's reading diāo, sharing a similar final.

example.hanzi: 貂皮大衣很保暖也很贵。
example.pinyin: Diāopí dàyī hěn bǎonuǎn yě hěn guì.
example.english: A sable fur coat is very warm but also very expensive.
example.fact: Sable fur has long been prized as one of the warmest natural furs — historically in Russia it was so valuable that sable pelts were sometimes used as a form of tribute payment or currency.

components.note: 虫 (a radical used broadly for creatures) — 蜥 names the lizard.
析 (xī) gives the sound — 蜥 is also pronounced xī, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 蜥蜴可以在沙漠中生存。
example.pinyin: Xīyì kěyǐ zài shāmò zhōng shēngcún.
example.english: Lizards can survive in the desert.
example.fact: Some lizard species can detach their own tail when caught by a predator — a defense called autotomy — and later regrow a new, though usually shorter, replacement tail.

meanings: to move carefully, as if evading a danger
etymologyHint: A broken 敝 foot 足; 敝 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Foot — relates to limping or a hurt ankle.
敝 is read bì, only loosely similar to bié (shares the initial b- but not the full syllable) — an approximate resemblance, not a close match. It also means 'worn out, broken,' fitting a lame gait.

example.pinyin: Tā jiǎng de Yīngyǔ hěn biéjiǎo.
example.english: His spoken English is clumsy.
example.fact: 蹩脚, literally 'a limping foot,' is commonly used figuratively in Mandarin to describe something done clumsily or a skill practiced poorly, as in 蹩脚的英语 ('broken English').

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噼 is an onomatopoeia for a cracking or popping sound.
辟 (here read pì) gives the sound — 噼 is pronounced pī, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Biānpào pīpā zuò xiǎng.
example.english: The firecrackers crackled and popped.
example.fact: Firecrackers were originally made in ancient China by burning bamboo stalks, which pop loudly as their hollow segments heat up and burst — a practice that gave firecrackers their Chinese name, 爆竹 ('exploding bamboo').

components.note: 钅 (metal) — titanium is a metallic element.
太 (tài) gives the sound — 钛 is also pronounced tài, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 钛是一种又轻又坚固的金属。
example.pinyin: Tài shì yī zhǒng yòu qīng yòu jiāngù de jīnshǔ.
example.english: Titanium is a metal that is both light and strong.
example.fact: Titanium has the highest strength-to-weight ratio of any metal, which is why it's widely used in aerospace engineering, medical implants, and high-performance sports equipment.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — plutonium is a metallic element.
不 (bù) gives the sound — 钚 is also pronounced bù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 钚是一种放射性金属元素。
example.pinyin: Bù shì yī zhǒng fàngshèxìng jīnshǔ yuánsù.
example.english: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element.
example.fact: Plutonium barely exists in nature; nearly all of it is artificially produced in nuclear reactors, and it was first synthesized in 1940 by a team at the University of California, Berkeley.

components.note: 犭 (dog/animal) — 獾 names the badger.
雚 (here read huán) gives the sound — 獾 is pronounced huān, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Huān xǐhuan zài yèjiān huódòng.
example.english: Badgers like to be active at night.
example.fact: Badgers are powerful diggers that create extensive underground burrow systems called setts, which can be used by successive generations of badgers for decades or even centuries.

meanings: name of a river in Hunan

components.note: 氵 (water) — 濂 names a stream or waterfall.
廉 (lián) gives the sound — 濂 is also pronounced lián, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 周敦颐被称为濂溪先生。
example.pinyin: Zhōu Dūnyí bèi chēng wéi Liánxī xiānshēng.
example.english: Zhou Dunyi was known as "Mr. Lianxi."
example.fact: Zhou Dunyi, the Song-dynasty philosopher who helped found Neo-Confucianism, took his honorary name 濂溪先生 from a stream near his hometown; his short essay 《爱莲说》 praising the lotus is still studied in Chinese schools today.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — armor (铠) was traditionally made of metal.
岂 (here read kǎi) gives the sound — 铠 is also pronounced kǎi, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǔshì chuān zhe kǎijiǎ shàng zhànchǎng.
example.english: The warrior wore armor onto the battlefield.
example.fact: Ancient Chinese armor evolved from leather and lacquered plates in the Warring States period to lamellar iron and stitched iron-plate designs by the Han and Tang dynasties, growing lighter and more flexible over time.

components.note: 白 (white) — 皙 describes fair, pale skin.
析 (xī) gives the sound — 皙 is also pronounced xī, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā pífū báixī.
example.english: Her skin is fair.
example.fact: 白皙 pairs two near-synonyms for 'white, fair': 白 is one of the most ancient, frequently used color characters, while 皙 is a rarer, more literary term reserved mostly for describing skin tone.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霭 describes mist or haze, a weather phenomenon.
谒 (yè) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to ǎi.

example.pinyin: Bàngwǎn shānjiān mímàn zhe mù'ǎi.
example.english: In the evening, mist filled the mountains.
example.fact: Mist forms when water vapor condenses into tiny droplets suspended in the air; unlike fog, mist is typically thinner and reduces visibility less severely.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲈 names the perch/sea bass.
卢 (lú) gives the sound — 鲈 is also pronounced lú, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Lúyú shì chángjiàn de shíyòng yú.
example.english: Sea bass is a commonly eaten fish.
example.fact: The idiom 莼鲈之思 ('longing for water-shield soup and perch') comes from a Jin-dynasty official named Zhang Han, who resigned his post after being reminded of his hometown's local dishes — it is still used to express nostalgic homesickness.

components.note: 叵 is visually the mirror image of 可 (kě, 'can') — flipping the character reverses its meaning to 'cannot.' The resemblance to a container 匚 plus 口 is coincidental, not how the character actually arose.

example.pinyin: Zhège rén xīnhuái pǒcè.
example.english: This person harbors unfathomable, possibly sinister intentions.
example.fact: 叵 is one of the rare Chinese characters formed simply by mirroring another character — it is 可 ('can') written backward, and fittingly its meaning reverses to 'cannot' in words like 居心叵测.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霾 describes atmospheric haze, grouped with weather phenomena like rain.
貍 (lí) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to mái.

example.pinyin: Chéngshì lǐ wùmái yánzhòng.
example.english: The smog in the city is severe.
example.fact: 雾霾, the Chinese term for smog, combines 雾 (fog) and 霾 (dust haze); the character 霾 became far more common in Chinese media starting in the early 2010s as urban air pollution became a widely discussed public health issue.

meanings: (bound form) to vanish; to die out; to obliterate

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泯 describes something dissolving away.
民 (mín) gives the sound — 泯 is pronounced mǐn, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā tóngxīn wèi mǐn.
example.english: He has retained his childlike innocence.
example.fact: 童心未泯 ('one's childlike heart has not yet vanished') is a common compliment in Mandarin for an adult who keeps a playful, curious spirit despite growing older.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 碴 describes a chipped fragment, e.g. of stone or glass.
查 (here read chá) gives the sound — 碴 is also pronounced chá, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā zǒng shì zhǎo chár chǎojià.
example.english: He always looks for excuses to pick fights.
example.fact: 找碴儿, literally 'to look for a chipped edge,' is used figuratively to mean deliberately seeking out faults in someone to start an argument — everyday physical imagery turned into idiomatic speech.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸵 names the ostrich.
它 (tā) gives a sound only loosely related to 鸵's reading tuó, sharing the initial t-.

example.hanzi: 鸵鸟是世界上最大的鸟。
example.pinyin: Tuóniǎo shì shìjiè shàng zuìdà de niǎo.
example.english: The ostrich is the largest bird in the world.
example.fact: Ostriches are the largest living birds and can run at speeds up to about 70 kilometers per hour, making them the fastest animals on two legs.

etymologyHint: A mountain 山 by a valley 谷; 谷 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Mountain.
Valley — directly matches 峪's meaning. Its reading gǔ is not close to yù, so it does not indicate the sound.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo shānyù fēngjǐng yōuměi.
example.english: This mountain valley has beautiful scenery.
example.fact: 峪 appears almost exclusively in place names for narrow mountain valleys across northern China, where it typically combines with a family name or descriptive word to label one specific ravine.

components.note: 食 (eat/food) — 饕 describes gluttony.
號 (here read háo) gives a sound only loosely related to 饕's reading tāo, sharing the final -ao.

example.hanzi: 这次聚餐简直是一场饕餮盛宴。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì jùcān jiǎnzhí shì yī chǎng tāotiè shèngyàn.
example.english: This dinner gathering was truly a sumptuous feast.
example.fact: 饕餮 originally named a mythical monster famous for its insatiable appetite; its stylized face motif appears carved on ritual bronze vessels from the Shang dynasty, over 3,000 years old.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘁 describes being worn out and exhausted, as if ill.
卒 (here read cù) gives a sound close to 瘁's reading cuì, sharing the initial c-.

example.pinyin: Tā wèile gōngzuò xīnlì jiāo cuì.
example.english: He is mentally and physically exhausted because of work.
example.fact: 鞠躬尽瘁，死而后已 ('bow in service, spare no effort, until death') comes from a memorial by the strategist Zhuge Liang expressing total devotion to his ruler's cause, and remains a byword for selfless dedication.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睢 describes staring, an action of the eyes.
隹 (zhuī) gives a sound close to 睢's reading suī, sharing the final -ui.

example.pinyin: Suīyáng céng shì zhòngyào de gǔchéng.
example.english: Suiyang was once an important ancient city.
example.fact: Suiyang was the site of a famous ten-month siege during the An Lushan Rebellion in 757 AD, where the Tang general Zhang Xun's desperate defense against overwhelming odds became legendary in Chinese history.

components.note: 髟 (hair) — 鬃 names a mane, made of hair.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — 鬃 is also pronounced zōng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Mǎzōng zài fēng zhōng piāodòng.
example.english: The horse's mane fluttered in the wind.
example.fact: A horse's mane, made of the protein keratin, serves practical purposes beyond looks — it helps protect the neck from insect bites and regulates temperature.

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — ties to distance traveled, fitting 迩's meaning 'near, close by.'
尔 (ěr) gives the sound — 迩 is also pronounced ěr, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng wénmíng xiá'ěr.
example.english: This restaurant is famous far and near.
example.fact: 闻名遐迩 pairs 遐 ('far') and 迩 ('near') as an antonym set meaning 'known both far and near' — pairing opposite characters like this is a common way Chinese idioms express totality.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 纣 originally referred to part of a harness or saddle strap.
寸 (cùn) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to zhòu.

example.hanzi: 商纣王是历史上著名的暴君。
example.pinyin: Shāng Zhòu Wáng shì lìshǐ shàng zhùmíng de bàojūn.
example.english: King Zhou of Shang was a notorious tyrant in history.
example.fact: King Zhou, the Shang dynasty's final ruler around the 11th century BC, became a stock example of tyranny in Chinese historiography and was ultimately overthrown by King Wu, an event traditionally marking the founding of the Zhou dynasty.

meanings: one-legged mountain demon of Chinese mythology
etymologyHint: A monster with a face, a nose 自, and one foot 夊

components.note: Represents the grotesque face of this mythical one-legged mountain demon.
Represents its single leg — ancient bronze art traditionally depicts the 夔 creature with just one leg.

example.hanzi: 夔纹是青铜器上常见的装饰图案。
example.pinyin: Kuíwén shì qīngtóngqì shàng chángjiàn de zhuāngshì tú'àn.
example.english: The kui pattern is a decorative motif commonly seen on bronze vessels.
example.fact: 夔纹, a stylized dragon-like motif with a single leg, is one of the most common decorative patterns on ancient Chinese bronze ritual vessels from the Shang and Zhou dynasties, alongside the similarly famous taotie face motif.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 垠 describes the boundary or edge of land.
艮 (gèn) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to yín.

example.pinyin: Shāmò yī wàng wú yín.
example.english: The desert stretches out boundlessly.
example.fact: 一望无垠 ('boundless at a glance') is a common phrase in Chinese descriptive writing for vast, flat landscapes like deserts or grasslands — 垠 almost always appears negated as 无垠 ('without limit') rather than standing alone.

meanings: used in 餛飩|馄饨[hun2 tun5]

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饨 (as in 馄饨) names a type of stuffed dumpling.
屯 (tún) gives the sound — 饨 is also pronounced tún, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zǎocān xǐhuan chī húntun.
example.english: I like to eat wontons for breakfast.
example.fact: Wonton is one of the oldest known dumpling dishes in China, and different regions have their own names for similar versions of it, such as 抄手 in Sichuan and 云吞 in Cantonese.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 榭 names a wooden garden pavilion.
射 (shè) gives a sound close to 榭's reading xiè, sharing the tone and a similar final.

example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ yǒu yī zuò shuǐxiè.
example.english: There's a waterside pavilion in the garden.
example.fact: 水榭, open-sided wooden structures built at the edge of a pond, are a signature feature of classical Chinese gardens, designed to let visitors enjoy views of the water and lotus flowers from a shaded platform.

components.note: 阝 (place, from 阜 'mound/earthworks') — 隍 describes a dry moat, an earthwork.
皇 (huáng) gives the sound — 隍 is also pronounced huáng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Hěn duō chéngshì dōu yǒu Chénghuáng Miào.
example.english: Many cities have City God temples.
example.fact: The City God (城隍) is a guardian deity in traditional Chinese folk religion believed to protect a specific city and oversee the souls of its deceased residents; nearly every walled city in imperial China had its own City God temple.

components.note: 女 (woman) — several characters describing graceful movement or dance use the woman radical.
沙 (shā) gives a sound only loosely related to 娑's reading suō, sharing the initial s-/sh-.

example.pinyin: Shùyè zài fēng zhōng pósuō qǐwǔ.
example.english: The leaves swayed and danced in the wind.
example.fact: 婆娑 describes the graceful swaying motion of dancing figures, tree branches, or shadows, and functions as a single inseparable descriptive unit rather than two independently meaningful words.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 篝 names a bamboo frame or cage.
冓 (gòu) gives the sound — 篝 is pronounced gōu, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tóngxuémen wéi zhe gōuhuǒ chànggē.
example.english: The classmates sang songs around the campfire.
example.fact: 篝火 (campfire) originally referred to a fire built inside or under a bamboo frame or cage used to dry clothes; the meaning later broadened to describe any open outdoor bonfire.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 榔 names a type of tree, as in 槟榔 (betel palm).
郎 (láng) gives the sound — 榔 is also pronounced láng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 槟榔在东南亚很受欢迎。
example.pinyin: Bīnláng zài Dōngnányà hěn shòu huānyíng.
example.english: Betel nut is very popular in Southeast Asia.
example.fact: Betel nut is chewed as a mild stimulant across parts of Southeast and South Asia, but the World Health Organization classifies it as a Group 1 carcinogen due to its strong association with oral cancer.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洌 describes clear, pure water.
列 (liè) gives the sound — 洌 is also pronounced liè, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shānquán shuǐ qīngliè gāntián.
example.english: The mountain spring water is clear, pure, and sweet.
example.fact: 洌 and its near-homophone 烈 (fierce, strong, as in strong liquor) are often confused by learners because they share a phonetic component and identical pronunciation, despite having completely different radicals — water 氵 versus fire 灬.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浜 names a small creek.
兵 (bīng) gives a sound only loosely related to 浜's reading bāng, sharing the initial b- and final -ng.

example.pinyin: Shànghǎi yǒu hěn duō xiǎo bāng.
example.english: Shanghai has many small creeks.
example.fact: 浜, meaning a small creek, appears in many place names around Shanghai and the Yangtze Delta, reflecting the historically dense network of canals that once crisscrossed the area before much of it was filled in during modern urbanization.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲑 names the salmon.
圭 (guī) gives the sound — 鲑 is also pronounced guī, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Guīyú huì nìliú ér shàng chǎnluǎn.
example.english: Salmon swim upstream against the current to spawn.
example.fact: Salmon are famous for navigating back to the exact stream where they were born to spawn, sometimes traveling thousands of kilometers using a combination of magnetic-field sensing and smell to find their way home.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谔 describes speaking out frankly.
咢 (è) gives the sound — 谔 is also pronounced è, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xiànglái zhíyán è'è.
example.english: He has always spoken frankly and boldly.
example.fact: The line '千人之诺诺，不如一士之谔谔' ('a thousand yes-men are worth less than one outspoken critic'), traditionally traced to the historian Sima Qian, is still quoted today to praise honest dissent over empty flattery.

etymologyHint: The sound 曰 of a stream 氵

components.note: Water — a rushing stream.
Originally associated with speech/sound; here it suggests the gurgling sound of rushing water rather than indicating the reading (曰 is read yuē, unrelated to gǔ).

example.pinyin: Quánshuǐ gǔgǔ de liúchū.
example.english: The spring water gushed out with a gurgling sound.
example.fact: 汩汩 imitates the gurgling sound of flowing water. Despite looking almost identical, 汩 (gǔ) is frequently confused with 汨 (mì) — a different character with a shorter middle stroke — even by native Chinese speakers.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浣 means to wash or rinse with water.
完 (wán) gives the sound — 浣 is pronounced huàn, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Xīshī zài jiāngbiān huànshā.
example.english: Xi Shi washed silk by the riverside.
example.fact: "Xi Shi washing silk by the river" is a famous legend about one of ancient China's renowned beauties, and the story is often given as the origin of the place name Huansha, in present-day Zhejiang province.

components.note: 舌 (tongue) — 舐 means to lick with the tongue.
氏 (here read shì) gives the sound — 舐 is also pronounced shì, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Lǎo niú shì dú, chōngmǎn mǔ'ài.
example.english: The old cow licking its calf is full of maternal love.
example.fact: 老牛舐犊 ('an old cow licking its calf') is a Chinese idiom for deep parental devotion, based on real cattle behavior — cows lick their newborn calves clean to strengthen the maternal bond right after birth.

meanings: to watch from a height or distance

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞭 relates to watching and seeing clearly.
尞 (liáo) gives the sound — 瞭 is pronounced liǎo, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Shìbīng zài liàowàngtǎ shàng fàngshào.
example.english: The soldier kept watch from the watchtower.
example.fact: 瞭 has two pronunciations: liǎo, an older alternate form of 了 meaning 'to understand clearly,' and liào, used in words like 瞭望 ('to watch from a distance') — its eye radical 目 fittingly connects both senses to vision.

components.note: 忄 (heart/emotion) — 忻 describes a feeling of joy.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound close to 忻's reading xīn, sharing the final -in.

example.hanzi: 忻州是山西省的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Xīnzhōu shì Shānxī shěng de yī gè chéngshì.
example.english: Xinzhou is a city in Shanxi province.
example.fact: Xinzhou, a city whose name uses this character meaning 'joyful,' lies near Mount Wutai, one of the four sacred Buddhist mountains of China and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咻 describes shouting or calling out.
休 (xiū) gives the sound — 咻 is also pronounced xiū, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xiūxiū de chuǎnzhe qì.
example.english: He panted heavily, breathing "xiu xiu."
example.fact: The idiom 一傅众咻 ('one tutor, but a crowd shouting him down') comes from Mencius and describes how good instruction can be undone when surrounded by too many bad influences.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹑 names the quail.
享 (xiǎng) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to chún.

example.pinyin: Ānchún dàn hěn xiǎo dàn hěn yíngyǎng.
example.english: Quail eggs are small but very nutritious.
example.fact: Quail eggs are much smaller than chicken eggs — roughly a fifth the size — but proportionally contain more protein, iron, and vitamins per gram.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical is often used in characters for chemical terms and loanwords without carrying a specific sense.
坐 (zuò) gives the sound — 唑 is also pronounced zuò, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 咪唑是一种重要的化学物质。
example.pinyin: Mǐzuò shì yī zhǒng zhòngyào de huàxué wùzhì.
example.english: Imidazole is an important chemical substance.
example.fact: The suffix 唑 denotes azole compounds in Chinese chemical naming — five-membered nitrogen-containing rings — and appears in many antifungal drug names, since azole-based medicines are among the most common treatments for fungal infections.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 懋 describes diligence and striving, qualities of the heart and mind.
楙 (mào) gives the sound — 懋 is also pronounced mào, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古人常用懋字来赞美德行。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén cháng yòng mào zì lái zànměi déxíng.
example.english: Ancient people often used the character 懋 to praise virtuous conduct.
example.fact: 懋勤殿 ('Hall of Diligent Cultivation'), a hall in Beijing's Forbidden City, takes its name from this character meaning 'to strive diligently' — the hall once served as an imperial study and library for Qing-dynasty emperors.

components.note: 白 (white) — 皎 describes bright whiteness, especially of moonlight.
交 (jiāo) gives the sound — 皎 is pronounced jiǎo, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn yuèguāng jiǎojié.
example.english: Tonight the moonlight is bright and clear.
example.fact: 皎洁 is a favorite word in classical Chinese poetry for bright, pure moonlight, appearing in the famous line "明月何皎皎" ('how bright and clear the moon is') from the ancient anthology 古诗十九首.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诒 describes verbally passing something down.
台 (tái) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to yí.

example.hanzi: 祖先把智慧诒留给后人。
example.pinyin: Zǔxiān bǎ zhìhuì yí liú gěi hòurén.
example.english: The ancestors passed their wisdom down to later generations.
example.fact: 诒 is a variant form of the more common character 贻, both meaning 'to bequeath, pass down' — such variant pairs, differing only in radical (言 versus 贝), are common among characters describing acts of giving.

components.note: Feather/hair — military command banners were often adorned with feathers or animal-hair tassels.

example.hanzi: 士兵们都是将军麾下的精兵。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen dōu shì jiāngjūn huīxià de jīngbīng.
example.english: The soldiers are all elite troops under the general's command.
example.fact: 麾下 ('beneath the banner') is a classical term still used today as a respectful way to refer to someone serving under a military commander, evoking troops standing beneath their general's command flag.

components.note: 车 (vehicle/wheel) — 辏 describes spokes converging at a wheel's hub.
奏 (zòu) gives a sound close to 辏's reading còu, sharing the final -ou and a related affricate initial.

example.hanzi: 这里商贾辐辏，十分繁华。
example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ shānggǔ fúcòu, shífēn fánhuá.
example.english: Here merchants converge as if toward a hub, making it extremely bustling.
example.fact: 辐辏, literally describing how a wheel's spokes converge at its hub, is used in classical Chinese economic writing to describe merchants, goods, and trade routes all converging on one prosperous city.

components.note: 氏 (clan) — 氐 relates to lineage and tribal identity, as an ancient ethnic name.

example.hanzi: 氐族是中国古代的一个民族。
example.pinyin: Dīzú shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de yī gè mínzú.
example.english: The Di people were an ancient ethnic group in China.
example.fact: The Di people founded several regional states during China's Sixteen Kingdoms period (4th–5th century AD), including the Former and Later Qin states in what is now northwestern China.

components.note: 冫 (ice) — 冽 describes bitterly cold weather.
列 (liè) gives the sound — 冽 is also pronounced liè, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Dōngtiān de hánfēng shífēn lǐnliè.
example.english: The winter wind is extremely cold and biting.
example.fact: 冽 (cold, biting) and 洌 (clear, pure water) are a classic pair of nearly identical Mandarin characters, sharing the same pronunciation and phonetic component but differing only in radical — ice 冫 versus water 氵.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — a winnowing basket/dustpan (箕) was traditionally woven from bamboo.
其 (qí) gives a sound close to 箕's reading jī, sharing the final -i.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng jī lái fēnlí gǔké.
example.english: Farmers use a winnowing basket to separate grain husks.
example.fact: 箕 lends its shape to the star name 箕宿, one of the 28 traditional constellations used in ancient Chinese astronomy to track the moon's path across the sky.

meanings: old name for the 黎[Li2] ethnic group

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俚 describes the unrefined speech of common people.
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 俚 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè jù huà shì dāngdì de lǐyǔ.
example.english: This phrase is local slang.
example.fact: 俚语 (slang) traditionally carried a slightly dismissive connotation, since 俚 originally described the unrefined speech of commoners as opposed to the formal literary language used by the educated elite in imperial China.

meanings: name of a river in Henan

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汴 names a river.
