卞 (biàn) gives the sound — 汴 is also pronounced biàn, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Biànliáng shì Sòngcháo de dūchéng.
example.english: Bianliang was the capital of the Song dynasty.
example.fact: Bianliang, an old name for present-day Kaifeng, was the capital of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127) and possibly the largest and most prosperous city in the world at the time, with a population that may have exceeded one million.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宸 refers to a palace, a roofed imperial dwelling.
辰 (chén) gives the sound — 宸 is also pronounced chén, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 宸常用来指皇帝居住的宫殿。
example.pinyin: Chén cháng yòng lái zhǐ huángdì jūzhù de gōngdiàn.
example.english: Chen is often used to refer to the palace where the emperor resides.
example.fact: 宸 is an elevated, literary term reserved almost exclusively for the emperor's residence or, by extension, the emperor himself — such words formed a special vocabulary tier used only in formal, reverential contexts involving the throne.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 芍 names the peony.
勺 (sháo) gives the sound — 芍 is also pronounced sháo, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Sháoyao huā zài wǔyuè shèngkāi.
example.english: Peony flowers bloom in full in May.
example.fact: The Chinese peony was traditionally given as a parting gift between friends, since ancient poetry associated it with farewell — unlike the related tree peony (牡丹), which instead symbolized wealth and honor.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — shared with its near-synonym 挨; the connection to 'endure' isn't a literal hand action, since radicals can group variant characters rather than reflect a literal meaning.
厓 (yá) gives a sound only loosely related to 捱's reading ái.

example.hanzi: 他捱过了最艰难的时期。
example.pinyin: Tā ái guò le zuì jiānnán de shíqī.
example.english: He endured through the most difficult period.
example.fact: 捱 is a variant form of the more common character 挨, both meaning 'to endure' or 'to get through' hard times, as in 捱过/挨过 — the two are used interchangeably in most contexts today.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摈 describes pushing something away, a hand action.
宾 (bīn) gives the sound — 摈 is pronounced bìn, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 我们应该摈弃陈旧的观念。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi bìnqì chénjiù de guānniàn.
example.english: We should discard outdated ideas.
example.fact: 摈弃 ('to cast aside') pairs two near-synonymous characters for rejection, a common intensifying pattern in Mandarin where similar-meaning characters combine to form a stronger, more formal two-character word.

etymologyHint: Skill 習 in paper-folding扌 ; 習 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand — folding is done by hand.
Originally related to the repeated motion of a bird folding and unfolding its wings, extended to 'folding.' Its reading xí is not close to zhé, so it contributes meaning here, not sound.

example.pinyin: Dàchén chéng shàng yī fèn zòuzhé.
example.english: The minister submitted a memorial to the throne.
example.fact: 奏摺 memorials were the standard format Qing-dynasty officials used to report to the emperor; the character 摺 reflects their physical form as folded documents, and thousands of the originals survive in the Beijing and Taipei palace museum archives.

meanings: large umbrella with a long handle
an ancient kind of bamboo or straw hat

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — an ancient long-handled umbrella (簦) was made from bamboo.
登 (dēng) gives the sound — 簦 is also pronounced dēng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古代旅人常背着簦遮阳挡雨。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài lǚrén cháng bēi zhe dēng zhē yáng dǎng yǔ.
example.english: Ancient travelers often carried a long-handled umbrella to shield themselves from sun and rain.
example.fact: 簦, an ancient umbrella with a long handle that could be worn like a hat while leaving the hands free, was historically associated with traveling scholars and commoners, unlike the canopy-style umbrella reserved for nobles riding in carriages.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 箔 originally referred to woven bamboo or reed matting, later extended to thin sheets like foil.
泊 (here read bó) gives the sound — 箔 is also pronounced bó, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Gōngjiàng bǎ huángjīn dǎ chéng jīnbó.
example.english: Craftsmen hammer gold into gold foil.
example.fact: Gold foil can be hammered so thin — sometimes under a tenth of a micrometer — that it becomes almost transparent, letting light pass through with a faint greenish tint.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咝 is an onomatopoeia for a hissing sound made with the mouth.
丝 (sī) gives the sound — 咝 is also pronounced sī, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Kāishuǐhú sīsī de xiǎng.
example.english: The kettle hissed.
example.fact: 咝 imitates a hissing sound, and its pronunciation sī itself carries a similar hissing quality — an example of sound symbolism, where a word's pronunciation echoes the sound it describes.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 孀 specifically names a widow.
霜 (shuāng) gives the sound — 孀 is also pronounced shuāng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā niánqīng shí jiù shuāngjū.
example.english: She became a widow while still young.
example.fact: 孀 is a specialized, literary character referring exclusively to a widow, distinct from the more general term 寡妇, and it appears almost only in formal or classical writing rather than everyday conversation.

components.note: 忄 (heart/emotion) — 怏 describes a feeling of displeasure.
央 (yāng) gives the sound — 怏 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā yàngyàng bù lè de líkāi le.
example.english: He left looking sulky and displeased.
example.fact: 怏怏不乐 uses a reduplicated form of 怏 to intensify the description of sulky displeasure — reduplication, repeating a character to strengthen its meaning, is a common technique in Mandarin.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谝 means to chat idly or brag verbally.
扁 (here read piān) gives the sound — 谝 is pronounced piǎn, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan gēn péngyǒu piǎn xiánhuà.
example.english: He likes to chat idly with friends.
example.fact: 谝 is especially common in Shaanxi and other northwestern Mandarin dialects, where 谝闲话 means casual chatting — a reminder that standard vocabulary lists don't capture the many words specific to China's regional dialects.

components.note: 石 (stone) — an anvil or chopping block (砧) was traditionally made of stone.
占 (here read zhān) gives a sound only loosely related to 砧's reading zhēn, sharing the initial zh-.

example.pinyin: Māma zài zhēnbǎn shàng qiē cài.
example.english: Mom is cutting vegetables on the chopping board.
example.fact: Traditional Chinese chopping boards were historically made from a single cross-section of a tree trunk, prized because the wood's circular grain pattern resists splitting better than boards cut lengthwise from a plank.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馕 names a type of flatbread.
囊 (náng) gives the sound — 馕 is also pronounced náng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xīnjiāng rén xǐhuan chī náng.
example.english: Xinjiang people like to eat naan bread.
example.fact: 馕, a round flatbread central to Uyghur cuisine in Xinjiang, is traditionally baked by slapping the dough onto the inner wall of a cylindrical clay oven called a tandoor — the same style of oven used across Central and South Asia.

components.note: 老 (old) — 耄 describes extreme old age.
毛 (máo) gives the sound — 耄 is pronounced mào, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Lǎorén yǐjīng nián guò màodié.
example.english: The elderly person is already well past eighty or ninety years old.
example.fact: In classical Chinese, specific decades of old age each had their own honorific term — 花甲 for sixty, 古稀 for seventy, and 耄耋 for eighty and ninety — reflecting the cultural importance placed on longevity.

components.note: 缶 (pottery/earthenware jar) — 罂 names a long-necked jar.

example.hanzi: 罂粟花很美丽，但也很危险。
example.pinyin: Yīngsù huā hěn měilì, dàn yě hěn wēixiǎn.
example.english: Poppy flowers are very beautiful, but also very dangerous.
example.fact: 罂粟 (opium poppy) takes its first character from 罂, an old word for a long-necked jar, because the plant's seed pod — scored to harvest raw opium — resembles a small jar in shape.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漕 relates to water transport, shipping grain by canal.
曹 (cáo) gives the sound — 漕 is also pronounced cáo, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古代靠漕运把粮食运到京城。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài kào cáoyùn bǎ liángshí yùn dào jīngchéng.
example.english: In ancient times, grain was shipped to the capital via canal transport.
example.fact: 漕运 relied heavily on the Grand Canal, one of the world's oldest and longest artificial waterways, greatly expanded during the Sui dynasty around 605 AD, to move grain from the fertile south to feed the capital in the north.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沣 names a river.
丰 (fēng) gives the sound — 沣 is also pronounced fēng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Fēng Hé liújīng Xī'ān fùjìn.
example.english: The Feng River flows near Xi'an.
example.fact: The Feng River gave its name to Fengjing, one of two paired capitals — along with Haojing across the river — of the Western Zhou dynasty around the 11th century BC, forming one of ancient China's earliest twin-capital arrangements.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 栾 names an ornamental tree, the goldenrain tree.
亦 (yì) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to luán.

example.pinyin: Luánshù de huā shì jīnhuángsè de.
example.english: The goldenrain tree's flowers are golden yellow.
example.fact: The goldenrain tree produces clusters of yellow flowers in summer followed by distinctive papery, lantern-shaped seed pods, which is why in English it is sometimes also called the 'lantern tree.'

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 carpenter's square 矩; 矩 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Wood — the tool is made of wood.
矩 shares the exact same reading, jǔ, as this character. It also means 'carpenter's square' — 榘 is simply a variant way of writing 矩.

example.pinyin: Mùjiang yòng jǔ lái huà zhíjiǎo.
example.english: The carpenter uses a square to draw right angles.
example.fact: 榘 is a rare variant of the more common character 矩 ('carpenter's square'), which itself gives rise to the idiom 循规蹈矩 ('following rules and norms'), describing someone who strictly adheres to convention.

components.note: 火 (fire) — chemistry terms for combustible hydrocarbons conventionally use the fire radical.
完 (wán) gives the sound — 烷 is also pronounced wán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 甲烷是一种无色无味的气体。
example.pinyin: Jiǎwán shì yī zhǒng wúsè wúwèi de qìtǐ.
example.english: Methane is a colorless, odorless gas.
example.fact: Methane, the simplest alkane, is odorless in its pure form — the smell associated with natural gas leaks actually comes from a sulfur-based chemical called mercaptan that utility companies deliberately add as a safety measure.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 榷 originally referred to a wooden footbridge or checkpoint structure where tolls were collected.
隺 (hè) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to què.

example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí zhídé shāngquè.
example.english: This issue is worth further discussion.
example.fact: 商榷 ('to deliberate') traces back to 榷's original meaning of a government-controlled monopoly checkpoint — the imperial Chinese state historically ran monopolies on goods like salt and tea, taxing their trade at fixed stations called 榷场.

meanings: wooden figures buried with the dead

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俑 names a figurine representing a person, buried with the dead.
甬 (yǒng) gives the sound — 俑 is also pronounced yǒng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xī'ān yǒu hěn duō bīngmǎyǒng.
example.english: Xi'an has many terracotta warrior figurines.
example.fact: The Terracotta Army, discovered in 1974 near Xi'an, consists of over 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers buried to guard the tomb of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, and each figure has individually distinct facial features.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沱 names a river or stream.
它 (tā) gives a sound only loosely related to 沱's reading tuó, sharing the initial t-.

example.hanzi: 沱江是长江的支流之一。
example.pinyin: Tuó Jiāng shì Cháng Jiāng de zhīliú zhī yī.
example.english: The Tuo River is one of the tributaries of the Yangtze.
example.fact: 沱茶, a bowl-shaped compressed tea cake from Yunnan and Sichuan, takes its name from this character; its dense, compact shape was designed to make long-distance transport by mule caravan along the ancient Tea Horse Road easier.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 缜 originally described tightly, finely woven silk.
真 (zhēn) gives the sound — 缜 is pronounced zhěn, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā de tuīlǐ fēicháng zhěnmì.
example.english: His reasoning is extremely meticulous and rigorous.
example.fact: 缜密 uses the silk radical 纟 in 缜, since the character originally described finely and tightly woven silk thread — a concrete image later extended metaphorically to describe careful, detailed thinking.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹫 names the vulture/condor.
就 (jiù) gives the sound — 鹫 is also pronounced jiù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 秃鹫在高空盘旋寻找食物。
example.pinyin: Tūjiù zài gāokōng pánxuán xúnzhǎo shíwù.
example.english: The vulture circles high in the sky searching for food.
example.fact: Vultures have an exceptionally strong digestive system that lets them safely eat carrion carrying bacteria like anthrax and botulism, which are lethal to most other animals, thanks to their highly acidic stomachs.

meanings: kind of snail with spiral shell

components.note: 虫 (a radical used broadly for creatures, including mollusks) — 蛳 names a type of river snail.
师 (shī) gives a sound close to 蛳's reading sī, sharing the final -i and a related sibilant initial.

example.hanzi: 螺蛳粉是广西的特色小吃。
example.pinyin: Luósīfěn shì Guǎngxī de tèsè xiǎochī.
example.english: Luosifen is a specialty snack from Guangxi.
example.fact: 螺蛳粉 (river snail rice noodles), a pungent specialty from Liuzhou in Guangxi, became a huge online sensation in China in the late 2010s, with packaged versions selling widely despite — or perhaps partly because of — its famously strong smell.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剽 originally described armed robbery or plunder, an act involving weapons.
票 (piào) gives the sound — 剽 is pronounced piāo, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Tā yīn piāoqiè lùnwén bèi kāichú.
example.english: He was expelled for plagiarizing a paper.
example.fact: 剽窃 ('to plagiarize') originally described armed robbery or plunder in classical Chinese, and its meaning narrowed over time to specifically describe stealing someone else's written work or ideas.

components.note: 行 (walk/road) — 衢 describes a thoroughfare, a place for walking and travel.
瞿 (qú) gives the sound — 衢 is also pronounced qú, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 衢州是浙江省的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Qúzhōu shì Zhèjiāng shěng de yī gè chéngshì.
example.english: Quzhou is a city in Zhejiang province.
example.fact: Quzhou, a city whose name uses this character meaning 'thoroughfare,' has historically served as a strategic crossroads connecting Zhejiang, Fujian, Jiangxi, and Anhui provinces.

components.note: 氵 (water/bodily fluid) — 泗 describes nasal mucus, and separately names a river.
四 (sì) gives the sound — 泗 is also pronounced sì, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā kū de tìsì héngliú.
example.english: He cried until tears streamed down his face.
example.fact: 涕泗横流 ('tears and mucus flowing freely') is a vivid, slightly dramatic classical expression for crying uncontrollably, still used today in both serious and exaggerated storytelling.

meanings: to smell of urine (or sweat etc)

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 臊 describes a rank smell, often of meat.
喿 (here read sào) gives the sound — 臊 is pronounced sāo, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Yángròu yǒu yī zhǒng sāowèi.
example.english: Mutton has a rank, gamey smell.
example.fact: The gamey odor some people notice in mutton comes mainly from branched-chain fatty acids that build up more in older or intact male animals, which is why younger lamb typically smells milder than mature mutton.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘴 describes noxious vapors historically blamed for tropical disease.
章 (zhāng) gives the sound — 瘴 is pronounced zhàng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Gǔrén rènwéi nánfāng duō zhàngqì.
example.english: Ancient people believed the south had a lot of noxious vapors.
example.fact: Before the discovery of mosquito-borne transmission in the late 19th century, many cultures — including ancient China with its concept of 瘴气 ('miasma') — blamed diseases like malaria on bad air rather than insect bites.

components.note: 酉 (originally 'wine/fermented liquid,' repurposed in modern chemistry for organic compounds) — 酚 (phenol) is an organic chemical.
分 (fēn) gives the sound — 酚 is also pronounced fēn, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 苯酚是一种常见的化工原料。
example.pinyin: Běnfēn shì yī zhǒng chángjiàn de huàgōng yuánliào.
example.english: Phenol is a common industrial chemical.
example.fact: Phenol was one of the first antiseptics used in modern surgery — British surgeon Joseph Lister pioneered its use in the 1860s to sterilize wounds and instruments, dramatically reducing post-operative infection rates.

etymologyHint: A thread 纟 with some give 予; 予 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Thread/silk — relates to loosening a taut thread, i.e. easing tension.
Means 'to give' — contributes to the sense of 'giving way, easing up.' Its reading yǔ is not close to shū, so it does not indicate the sound.

example.hanzi: 两人达成协议，纾解了紧张关系。
example.pinyin: Liǎng rén dáchéng xiéyì, shūjiě le jǐnzhāng guānxì.
example.english: The two reached an agreement, easing their tense relationship.
example.fact: 纾解 combines 纾, whose silk radical 纟 originally suggested loosening a taut thread, with 解, meaning 'to untie or resolve' — together forming a common verb for easing tension of any kind.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晁's original meaning relates to morning and daybreak.
兆 (zhào) gives a sound close to 晁's reading cháo, sharing the final -ao and a related retroflex initial.

example.hanzi: 晁错是汉朝著名的政治家。
example.pinyin: Cháo Cuò shì Hàncháo zhùmíng de zhèngzhìjiā.
example.english: Chao Cuo was a famous statesman of the Han dynasty.
example.fact: Chao Cuo proposed reducing the power of regional feudal kings to strengthen central imperial authority — a policy that provoked a rebellion and led to his execution around 154 BC, despite the emperor later adopting similar reforms.

example.hanzi: 古书记载了一次星孛的出现。
example.pinyin: Gǔshū jìzǎi le yī cì xīngbèi de chūxiàn.
example.english: Ancient records documented the appearance of a comet.
example.fact: Ancient Chinese astronomers kept some of the world's most detailed and continuous comet records, including what many historians consider the earliest reliable record of Halley's Comet, dating to 240 BC.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炀 means to roast or melt with fire.
昜 (yáng) gives the sound — 炀 is also pronounced yáng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Suí Yángdì xiūjiàn le Dà Yùnhé.
example.english: Emperor Yang of Sui built sections of the Grand Canal.
example.fact: Emperor Yang of Sui is credited with completing major sections of the Grand Canal linking northern and southern China, though his reign is more often remembered for the forced labor and military campaigns that helped trigger the dynasty's collapse within decades.

etymologyHint: Three 三 with accents to prevent forgery

components.note: The base of 叁 is simply 三 ('three'); the elaborate strokes above are decorative additions with no meaning of their own, added purely to make the numeral harder to forge or alter on financial documents.

example.hanzi: 支票上要写"叁"而不是"三"。
example.pinyin: Zhīpiào shàng yào xiě "sān" ér búshì "sān".
example.english: On a check, one should write the formal "san" rather than the simple one.
example.fact: 叁 and 三 (both 'three') are pronounced identically, but 叁 — along with similar 'anti-fraud' numerals like 壹 and 贰 — is required on Chinese checks and contracts because its complex strokes are much harder to alter than the simple lines of 一, 二, and 三.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — to rest (憩) implies calming the heart and mind.
自 (zì) gives a sound only loosely related to 憩's reading qì, sharing the final -i.

example.hanzi: 我们在公园里休憩片刻。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài gōngyuán lǐ xiūqì piànkè.
example.english: We rested for a moment in the park.
example.fact: 休憩 pairs two near-synonyms for rest — 憩 itself rarely appears alone in modern speech and almost always shows up bonded to 休 in this fixed two-character form.

meanings: to grasp or hold with both hands
etymologyHint: To take 扌a handful 匊; 匊 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: Hand — the action of scooping or grasping.
匊 shares the exact same reading, jū, as this character. It also means 'to scoop with both hands,' closely matching 掬's meaning.

example.hanzi: 她笑容可掬地欢迎客人。
example.pinyin: Tā xiàoróng kějū de huānyíng kèrén.
example.english: She welcomed the guests with a beaming smile.
example.fact: 笑容可掬 ('a smile that could be scooped up with both hands') is a vivid idiom for an especially warm smile — 掬 itself is a measure word for a double handful, as in 一掬清泉 ('a double handful of spring water').

components.note: 木 (tree) — 椤 (as in 桫椤) names the tree fern.
罗 (luó) gives the sound — 椤 is also pronounced luó, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 桫椤是一种古老的树种。
example.pinyin: Suōluó shì yī zhǒng gǔlǎo de shùzhǒng.
example.english: The tree fern is an ancient type of tree.
example.fact: Tree ferns are living relatives of plants that flourished during the Jurassic period over 180 million years ago, making them among the closest things to a living dinosaur-era plant found in modern forests.

components.note: 口 (mouth, and by extension teeth) — 啮 means to bite or gnaw.
齿 (chǐ) is listed as the phonetic element, though its modern reading isn't obviously close to niè.

example.pinyin: Lǎoshǔ shì yī zhǒng nièchǐ dòngwù.
example.english: The mouse is a type of rodent.
example.fact: 啮齿动物 ('gnawing-tooth animals'), the Chinese term for rodents, reflects a real biological feature: rodent incisors never stop growing, so they must constantly gnaw on hard materials to keep them from overgrowing.
